market_context: United States/general English; refrigerated storage of cooked salmon
title: How long does cooked salmon last in the fridge?

seo.title: How long does cooked salmon last in the fridge?
seo.meta_description: Cooked salmon follows the general cooked-fish rule: 3–4 days refrigerated at 40 °F or below when chilled promptly after cooking.
seo.search_intent: Learn how many days cooked salmon keeps refrigerated and when to freeze leftovers.

excerpt: Cooked salmon can be refrigerated for 3–4 days at 40 °F (4 °C) or below under USDA guidance for cooked fish and seafood. Refrigerate it within about two hours after cooking and freeze portions early if they will not be used within that window.
content_html:
Salmon does not get a longer refrigerator window because it is oily fish. USDA's cooked-seafood guidance is 3–4 days at 40 °F/4 °C or below.

Count from the day it was cooked

Salmon cooked on Monday should generally be used by Thursday or Friday when it was chilled promptly and kept cold.

Refrigerate within two hours

Perishable foods should be chilled within about 2 hours, or within one hour above 90 °F. Shallow containers cool portions faster.

Smell does not extend the clock

Sour, rancid or ammonia-like odor is a discard sign. But normal smell on day five or six does not prove the salmon is still within safe storage guidance.

Can cooked salmon be eaten cold?

Yes, if it was cooked and stored safely. Reheating is not required for a cold salad or sandwich. When leftovers are reheated, USDA uses 165 °F as the target.

Freeze extra portions

USDA lists about 3 months as a best-quality target for cooked fish in the freezer. Freezing early usually preserves better quality than waiting until refrigerator day four.

How to count the 3–4 day window in real life

The safest way to use the refrigerator guideline is to count from the day the salmon was cooked, not from the day you first open the leftover container. If salmon is cooked on Monday evening and chilled promptly, Monday is day zero and the next several days make up the recommended refrigerator window. Writing the cooking date on the container removes the guesswork, especially when several leftovers are in the fridge at once.

Cooling technique matters because a hot, tightly packed mass loses heat slowly. A single salmon fillet can usually be refrigerated in a shallow container once the meal is over; a large tray of salmon should be divided into smaller portions so the center cools faster. Keep the refrigerator at 40°F (4°C) or below and avoid storing leftovers in the door, where temperatures fluctuate more with opening. The storage clock is only useful if the food was chilled promptly and remained cold.

Texture often changes before safety becomes obvious. Refrigerated salmon can dry slightly, and repeated reheating tends to make that more noticeable. Reheat only the portion you plan to eat and use gentler heat when possible. For a cold salad or sandwich, keep the salmon refrigerated until assembly and return unused portions quickly rather than letting the whole container sit on the counter.

If plans change, freezing earlier is better than waiting until the end of day four. Portioning cooked salmon before freezing makes it easier to thaw only what you need. Thaw frozen leftovers in the refrigerator rather than on the counter, and remember that freezing pauses deterioration; it does not erase poor handling that happened before freezing. A leftover that already spent too long warm should not be “saved” by putting it in the freezer.

The form of the leftover matters too. Salmon mixed into a creamy sauce or rice dish should be dated from the same original cooking event, and adding new ingredients does not extend the fish’s storage life. Smoked salmon follows different guidance from cooked salmon because it is a different product with its own processing and package instructions. Likewise, canned salmon should be treated according to whether the can is unopened or has been opened and transferred to the refrigerator. Keeping categories separate prevents the common mistake of applying one “salmon lasts X days” rule to every salmon product. For ordinary cooked fillets, patties or baked salmon, the simple 3–4 day refrigerator window remains the right home rule when cooling and refrigeration were handled correctly.

A useful date depends on good refrigeration before it

The 3–4 day guideline assumes the salmon was chilled promptly and stayed at 40 °F/4 °C or below. If it sat on the table for several hours first, that margin is not restored just by putting it in the refrigerator later. Time out of refrigeration and refrigerated storage are parts of the same handling history.

For better texture during reheating, gentle covered heat often works better than blasting the fish until it dries. Safety is checked by the temperature reached in the food; there is no benefit in heating far beyond it.

Use cooked salmon within 3–4 refrigerated days. Chill promptly and freeze what will not be eaten in that period.

faq.question: Can I eat cooked salmon after five days?
faq.answer: USDA's conservative cooked-seafood window is 3–4 days, so discarding it after five days is safer.

faq.question: Can leftover salmon be eaten cold?
faq.answer: Yes, if it was cooked and refrigerated safely and remains within the storage window.

faq.question: How long does cooked salmon keep frozen?
faq.answer: USDA lists about 3 months for best quality of cooked fish.
